items.title: Are We Thinking Correctly About AI Intelligence?
items.excerpt: Melanie Mitchell argues on Quanta's 'The Joy of Why' that large models are an 'alien intelligence' whose mechanisms differ fundamentally from human cognition, and that we should borrow psychology's experimental methods rather than benchmarks to measure what machines actually understand.
items.note: Published time from article:published_time via WebFetch. Gated FRESH.

items.source: EurekAlert! (Artificial Intelligence & Environment / South China Normal University)
items.title: The AI scientist arrives: autonomous agents are reshaping scientific discovery
items.excerpt: A review of three 2026 Nature-reported systems — the Empirical Research Assistant, The AI Scientist and MIRA — finds agents now generate ideas, write code, run experiments, draft manuscripts and even do automated peer review, while still producing hallucinated citations and irreproducible results.
items.note: datePublished 2026-08-19 from the release page via WebFetch; time-of-day from the syndicated feed timestamp. Gated FRESH.

items.title: Prominent AI startup rolls out virtual cell model in race to speed up science
items.excerpt: Palo Alto's GenBio AI, with Nobel laureate David Baker involved, unveiled AIDO Cell — a 'Google Earth for the human cell' that predicts how a whole cell's molecular machinery shifts when you knock out a gene or add a drug, extending the AlphaFold idea from single proteins to entire cells.
items.note: Published date from the article page via WebFetch (Aug 18, 2026); time from the publisher feed. Gated FRESH.

items.title: Scientists have designed a functioning virus from scratch using AI. What you need to know
items.excerpt: AI genome-design models produced hundreds of novel bacteriophage variants; of 285 synthesized designs, 16 were functioning viruses able to kill drug-resistant bacteria. It is the first demonstration that a generative model can write a viable genome end to end — and it has biosecurity researchers arguing about screening safeguards.
items.note: Published time from article:published_time via WebFetch. Gated FRESH.

items.title: Protecting Scientific Intent in AI-Enabled Labs by Not Letting AI Set the Mission
items.excerpt: Stanford's Le Cong argues that as AI agents take over more of the bench, humans must keep ownership of the objective, the constraints and the risk envelope: 'humans need to be in the lead throughout the process,' or self-driving labs optimize for plausible-looking results instead of true ones.
items.note: Published time from article:published_time via WebFetch. Gated FRESH.

items.title: AI Identifies Pre-existing Antimicrobial Antibody Profile That May Predict Immune Response to Vaccination
items.excerpt: Arizona State researchers found that the antibody fingerprint you already carry against common microbes predicts how strongly you will respond to a vaccine — a pattern only legible once AI was run across the biomarker panel, opening the door to pre-screening vaccine responders.
items.note: Published time from article:published_time via WebFetch. Gated FRESH.

items.title: Combining AI with experiments to solve real-world materials problems
items.excerpt: CuspAI has assembled a 45-organisation 'Materials Foundry' to actually synthesize and test what its models predict — its Kemira collaboration proposed 20 novel MOFs for stripping PFAS from water in six months instead of years. The team's point: prediction is now the easy part; synthesis and manufacturability are the bottleneck.
items.note: Published time 2026-08-12T14:58:00+01:00 from article:published_time via WebFetch, normalized to UTC. Gated FRESH.

items.title: AI could offer a shortcut for designing more efficient airplane wings
items.excerpt: A machine-learning surrogate for computational fluid dynamics lets engineers explore aerodynamic shapes at a fraction of the simulation cost, potentially collapsing the design-iteration loop for more fuel-efficient wings.
items.note: WebFetch is blocked for newscientist.com; published time taken from New Scientist's own RSS <pubDate> (first-party), not a search snippet. Gated FRESH.

items.title: AI firms are watermarking generated text – here's why it won't work
items.excerpt: AI companies are embedding statistical watermarks in generated text to make it detectable, but the underlying research shows the signal degrades under paraphrase, translation and light editing — a provenance problem that lands directly on peer review and academic integrity.
items.note: WebFetch blocked for newscientist.com; published time from New Scientist's own RSS <pubDate>. Gated FRESH.

items.title: The Telescope That Points Itself
items.excerpt: Rather than encoding astronomers' scheduling rules, researchers trained a deep-learning model on years of Dark Energy Survey decisions and let it drive the 570-megapixel Dark Energy Camera for two full observing campaigns — matching human observers while deciding far faster, a template for Rubin-era survey scheduling.
items.note: The page exposes no explicit meta timestamp; published time from Universe Today's own RSS <pubDate>, corroborated by the og:image filename stamp 20260810_224303. Gated FRESH.

items.title: The physics of novel computation: beyond bits and chips to spikes and spins
items.excerpt: With silicon nearing its physical limits and AI's energy appetite still climbing, physicists survey the alternatives now moving out of the lab — spintronic, neuromorphic and spike-based computing — and argue physics, not more transistors, is what gets AI past the wall.
items.note: Published time from article:published_time via WebFetch. Gated FRESH.

items.title: Blocc chemistry could automate molecular discovery and democratize access to new materials
items.excerpt: Martin Burke's 'blocc' chemistry builds molecules by iterative carbon–carbon bonding from standard blocks, making robotic synthesis and AI-guided discovery usable by non-specialists — and generating the modular datasets those models need. Early wins include top-in-class organic laser emitters and solar-cell materials.
items.note: Published time from article:published_time via WebFetch. Gated FRESH.

items.title: AI screens 100,000+ membrane combinations, predicting carbon capture performance within seconds
items.excerpt: A Koç University machine-learning framework evaluated more than 104,000 mixed-matrix membrane combinations and predicted the performance of the promising ones in seconds, turning a years-long carbon-capture materials search into a screening problem.
items.note: Published time from article:published_time via WebFetch (Aug 19, 2026); time-of-day from the phys.org feed. Gated FRESH.

items.title: Deep-learning approach rapidly predicts where metals bind within proteins
items.excerpt: Hokkaido University's PRIME locates metal-binding sites — 'a needle in a haystack' inside a large protein — in roughly 11 seconds, a step the field previously handled with slow structural analysis, with direct implications for enzyme design and drug targeting.
items.note: Published time from article:published_time via WebFetch (Aug 18, 2026); time-of-day from the phys.org feed. Gated FRESH.

items.title: Neural network approach makes AI uncertainty checks far more efficient
items.excerpt: McGill researchers built models that estimate their own uncertainty using about 33x fewer parameters than standard methods while holding predictive accuracy — making calibrated confidence cheap enough to run in scientific and clinical settings where a wrong-but-confident answer is the real failure mode.
items.note: Published time from article:published_time via WebFetch. Gated FRESH.

items.title: More is different when AI agent populations work together, study suggests
items.excerpt: Identical models reach opposite collective conclusions depending purely on how many of them are interacting, the study finds — meaning single-agent safety evaluation misses emergent behaviour that only appears above certain population thresholds.
items.note: Published time from article:published_time via WebFetch. Gated FRESH.

items.title: AI helps turn citizen photos into water-level data
items.excerpt: University at Buffalo researchers automated the reading of crowd-submitted photos of stream gauges, using targeted image preprocessing to reach 98% accuracy on station identification — converting a citizen-science photo stream into usable hydrological measurement.
items.note: Published time from article:published_time via WebFetch. Gated FRESH.

items.title: Paving the way for greener ammonia production
items.excerpt: MIT researchers used machine learning to search alloy space for catalysts that make electrochemical nitrogen reduction viable, targeting a replacement for the fossil-fuel-dependent Haber-Bosch process that has run essentially unchanged for a century.
